lead: An instrument landing system (ILS) lets an aircraft fly a straight, accurate descent to a runway that the crew cannot see. Two ground transmitters each define one angle: the localizer says whether the aircraft is left or right of the extended centreline, and the glide path (glideslope) says whether it is above or below the descent slope. The crew, or the autopilot, keeps two needles centred. ILS is the world's standard precision approach aid and the basis of automatic landing; the microwave landing system (MLS) was designed to remove its limits, and satellite augmentation now offers a third way.
prereq: You need the geometry of lines of position and point-source aids and DME ranging.

sections.h3: Why ILS is needed, and its parts

blocks.text: Visual approaches stop when cloud and fog hide the runway. A non-precision aid such as a VOR gives only a track, not a slope, so the crew must stay high until they see the ground. ILS gives both lateral and vertical guidance down to a decision height of 200 ft or less, and with the right aircraft and crew to touchdown. That is its need: safe landings in low visibility, at a steady, predictable path that air traffic control can sequence.

blocks.text: Selecting one localizer frequency tunes the paired glide path automatically. Each ground transmitter has a monitor that switches it off, or to a standby, if its beam moves out of tolerance, so a faulty ILS goes silent rather than lies. Approach lights carry the pilot through the last, visual segment.

Both transmitters radiate a carrier amplitude-modulated by two tones, 90 Hz and 150 Hz, from two overlapping antenna patterns. The receiver filters out the two tones and compares their depths of modulation m90 and m150 (each a fraction from 0 to 1). On the course line the two depths are equal.

blocks.where: DDM is the difference in depth of modulation; positive means the 150 Hz tone is stronger. DDM = 0 on the course line, and the needle deflection is proportional to DDM.

blocks.text: Localizer sense: seen from an approaching aircraft, 90 Hz predominates to the left of the centreline and 150 Hz to the right. Full-scale deflection is DDM 0.155, at the edge of a course sector about 2.5° each side; the sector is set so it is 210 m (700 ft) wide at the threshold, so a long runway gets a narrower angle.

Glide path sense: 90 Hz predominates above the path and 150 Hz below it. Full-scale deflection is DDM 0.175, at about 0.7° above or below a 3° path, so the sector is about 1.4° thick. A receiver well below the path sees strong 150 Hz and shows "fly up".

Because guidance comes from a difference of two depths on one carrier, it does not depend on how strong the received signal is. Approach categories set how low the crew may go before seeing the runway:

head: Category
Decision height
Runway visual range
rows: less than 175 m but not less than 50 m

blocks.text: A category describes the whole operation (ground equipment, aircraft, crew training), not the receiver alone.

sections.h3: Advantages and limits of ILS, and MLS

blocks.text: Advantages of ILS: one standard worldwide, so every airliner can use every ILS; a cheap, simple airborne receiver; guidance that grows more precise as the aircraft nears the runway; integrity monitoring on the ground; and support for automatic landing in CAT III.

Limits: one straight path per runway end; only 40 channels; beams bent by reflections from buildings, terrain and taxiing aircraft, so critical areas must be kept clear in low visibility; and false glide paths at steeper angles above the real one, which is why the glide path is captured from below.

The microwave landing system (MLS) works at 5031–5091 MHz with 200 channels. A narrow beam sweeps "to" and "fro" across the approach sector, and the receiver measures the time between the two passes: the angle follows from that time. Azimuth coverage is about ±40° and elevation up to 15°, so curved and segmented approaches are possible; precision DME (DME/P) gives range. MLS saw little civil use because ILS was already fitted and satellite methods arrived. Today GBAS (a ground station correcting GPS at one airport) and SBAS (corrections over a whole region) offer precision approaches; see satellite navigation.

examples.question: An aircraft on a 3° ILS glide path is 5.0 nm (along the ground) from the point where the glide path meets the runway. (a) What height should it be at? (b) Its glide path receiver measures DDM 0.05 with 150 Hz stronger. Full-scale DDM 0.175 corresponds to 0.7°. How far off the path is it, on which side, and by how many feet?
steps: Range in feet: 1 nm = 6076 ft, so 5.0 nm = 30381 ft.
Height on the path = range × tan 3° = 30381 × 0.05241 = 1592 ft (the rule of thumb is about 318 ft per nm).
150 Hz stronger on the glide path means below the path, so the needle says "fly up".
The aircraft is on a 2.8° line instead of 3°: height = 30381 × tan 2.8° = 1486 ft.
examples.answer: It should be at about 1592 ft; it is 0.20° below the path, about 106 ft low (at 1486 ft), and must fly up.

examples.question: A localizer antenna stands 3300 m from the threshold, and the course sector is set to 210 m wide at the threshold. (a) Find the half-angle of the sector. (b) The receiver reads DDM 0.08 with 90 Hz stronger; full scale is DDM 0.155. Find the angular deviation, the side, and the sideways offset when the aircraft is 10 km from the antenna.
steps: Half the sector width at the threshold is 105 m, so the half-angle = arctan(105 ÷ 3300) = 1.82°.
90 Hz stronger on the localizer means left of the centreline (seen from the aircraft), so the needle shows the centreline to the right: fly right.
Sideways offset at 10 km = 10 000 × tan 0.94° = 164 m.
examples.answer: The half-angle is 1.82°; the aircraft is 0.94° left of the centreline, about 164 m at 10 km, and must fly right.

traps: Localizer: 90 Hz left, 150 Hz right (seen from the approaching aircraft). Glide path: 90 Hz above, 150 Hz below. Mixing the two senses gives the wrong side.
Full scale is about ±2.5° on the localizer but only about ±0.7° on the glide path; the glide path sector is 1.4° thick in total.
DDM is a difference of two modulation depths, not a ratio of two signal strengths.
Marker beacons (75 MHz) give distance check points, not guidance; they never define the centreline or the slope.
CAT IIIA and IIIB may have no decision height; only CAT IIIC has no RVR limit either.

quiz.q: State the frequency bands of the ILS localizer and glide path, and how the two are tuned.
quiz.a: Localizer 108.10–111.95 MHz (VHF), glide path 329.15–335.00 MHz (UHF). The 40 glide path channels are paired with the localizer channels, so selecting the localizer frequency tunes both.

quiz.q: Give the decision height and RVR for CAT I and CAT II.
quiz.a: CAT I: DH not below 60 m (200 ft), RVR not less than 550 m. CAT II: DH 30 to 60 m (100 to 200 ft), RVR not less than 300 m.

quiz.q: Why does an ILS receiver use the difference in depth of modulation rather than signal strength?
quiz.a: Signal strength changes with range, antenna pattern and aircraft attitude. The difference of the 90 Hz and 150 Hz depths is set by the angle from the course line, because both tones ride on the same carrier; so the deviation stays correct whatever the strength.

quiz.q: An aircraft is on a 3° path at 2000 ft above the touchdown point. What distance from touchdown should DME show (ignore the slant)?
quiz.a: Distance = 2000 ÷ tan 3° = 38162 ft = 6.28 nm. Check with 318 ft per nm: 2000 ÷ 318 = 6.29 nm.

quiz.q: The glide path receiver reads DDM 0.175 with 90 Hz stronger. Where is the aircraft?
quiz.a: DDM 0.175 is full scale, so about 0.7° from the path; 90 Hz stronger means above the path. The needle is at the bottom of its scale: fly down.

quiz.q: Give two reasons MLS is less sensitive to its site than ILS.
quiz.a: At 5 GHz the antennas are small and narrow beams can be formed, so less energy reaches buildings and the ground; and the angle comes from the timing of a scanning beam, not from comparing amplitudes of two broad overlapping patterns that reflections can distort.

quiz.q: Why is the glide path always captured from below?
quiz.a: The antenna system also produces false glide paths at steeper angles above the real one. Approaching from below at the intercept altitude, the first path the aircraft meets is the real 3° one.

beyond: Not for the exam. ILS performance is checked by regular flight inspection with a specially equipped aircraft. GBAS approaches (GLS) are now flown at several major airports, and work on GBAS for CAT III is continuing. Search for "ILS critical area", "flight inspection" and "GBAS landing system".
